appraisal_events.evidence: Opening on the « positions en apparence imprenables » of the Guermantes that « avaient perdu leur inviolabilité », the passage shows the duke fixed in Odette's armchair; when he turns his beast's stare on her « celle-ci lui tenait tête », and « le vieux fauve dompté » remembers he is no longer free « dans ce Sahara » of the duchesse's house but « chez Mme de Forcheville, dans la cage du Jardin des Plantes »; Jupiter becomes « un risible Géronte », and « à peine était-il parti, elle allait en rejoindre d'autres ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator stages the duke's fall as a change of empire: the imperious Guermantes is now a caged, half-blind old man who cannot do without Odette, is faced down by her in her own room and deceived as soon as he leaves.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Odette trompait M. de Guermantes, et aussi le soignait, sans charme, sans grandeur. Elle était médiocre dans ce rôle comme dans tous les autres… elle ne savait pas les jouer. » Believing the narrator a great writer, « elle redevenait maintenant avec moi simple cocotte pour m'intéresser », telling romantic anecdotes whose warmth about « pauvre Charles » the narrator knows to be false: « sa franchise se mêlait de mensonges ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's verdict on Odette is unillusioned: whatever the part life gives her, she plays it without charm or grandeur, and her confidences are performances staged to supply an author with material.

appraisal_events.evidence: « M. de Guermantes ne gardait ses foudres que pour la duchesse ; sur les libres fréquentations de laquelle Mme de Forcheville ne manquait pas d'attirer l'attention irritée du duc. Aussi la duchesse était-elle fort malheureuse. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Odette keeps the duke's anger pointed at his wife by denouncing her acquaintances, and the passage records the result directly: the duchesse is the one who suffers in the household.

appraisal_events.evidence: « quand je vous voyais causer avec Gilberte de Saint-Loup. Ce n'est pas digne de vous. Pour moi c'est exactement rien, cette femme-là, ce n'est même pas une femme, c'est ce que je connais de plus factice et de plus bourgeois au monde », while she offers instead a private lunch with Rachel, « cent fois supérieure à tout ce qui est ici » — the narrator noting that « même à sa défense de l'actualité, la duchesse mêlait ses préjugés d'aristocrate », and that she lies more and more and follows the critics' taste ten years late.
appraisal_events.explanation: The duchesse annihilates her niece by marriage in a single phrase and crowns the actress in her place; the narration lets the verdict stand as a verdict while discrediting the judge who delivers it.

status_effects.explanation: He cannot do without Odette, is stared down by her in her own drawing-room, and is deceived without seeing it: the leverage in the relation has passed entirely to her.
She holds the tamed old lion's gaze until he subsides and does as she pleases the moment he goes, though his jealousy still keeps her half cloistered.
The narration judges her mediocre in every role she is given and her frankness shot through with lies.
She is the one denounced, thundered at and made « fort malheureuse » in a household where the mistress directs the husband's anger at the wife.

Her contempt for Gilberte is delivered in the same breath as the narrator's exposure of her: a woman grown steadily more untruthful, disowning old salons and repeating the art criticism of ten years before.
The reigning duchesse dismisses her as nothing, not even a woman, the most artificial and bourgeois thing she knows, and ranks the actress far above her.

ambiguities: The duchesse's reputation is left explicitly undecided: M. de Charlus claims her legend of purity covers « un nombre incalculable d'aventures habilement dissimulées » while « pour presque tout le monde » she has always been irreproachable, and the narrator says he cannot decide between the two — so this claim is not recorded as a status movement.
